utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vlahovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Dutertre will now continue his examination-in-chief. [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vlahovic, good afternoon. Yesterday, you spoke about the tensions between the Serb population and the Albanian population in the area of Gornji Ratis in the years preceding the conflict. You talked about the Serb population in the area, the fact that Serbs left the area and you said why. Then you spoke about specific incidents in which Serb people were made victims at the end of 1998, and then you started telling us about what happened to your parents. You said that on the Sunday you went to Sremska Kamenica to see your uncle who was in hospital, and if I'm correct, this was the 19th of April 1998. Then you said you returned to Gornji Ratis on the 20th, and that you spent the night of the 20th at your parents' in the house at Gornji Ratis, which means the night between the Monday, 20th, to the Tuesday, 21st. And then you said that you saw your parents for the last time on the 21st of April, 1998, this Tuesday, in Gornji Ratis. Yesterday, before we wrapped up, I had started a few questions which related to a few answers that you provided during your testimony. I'd like to begin from this starting point again. My first question will be as follows: You said that during the month of April, Serbs had left the area and only returned to feed their cattle. You explained that they didn't feel safe. And you also said that shooting could be heard from Glodjane. And at the very beginning of your testimony yesterday, on page 1546 of the transcript, line 15, you said - and I'm going to refer to the English version of the transcript, of course - you indicated that there was a training camp in Glodjane, and that in the afternoon automatic rifles could often be heard. My first question is as follows: From Albanian into English and from English into French, the term you used, which in English was "training camp," and I think I heard something else in French, may not have been translated as it should have. Now, could you please tell us what was in Glodjane? Was it a shooting area? Was it another term that you wanted to use to tell us what exactly was in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time what people were saying in Glodjane was that this was a training ground. At the time a policeman named Miodrag Otovic was killed in Glodjane, and Momo Stijovic was wounded there as well. It was late in the afternoon. Then early in the evening, you could hear sounds of shooting at Ratishe, automatic weapons firing as well. They were probably doing some target practice or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: By "training camp," you're talking or you mean a military training area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think, but I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Who was the policeman who was killed in Glodjane? Could you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sure I can. Miodrag Otovic. He worked at the Rznic police station. I think he's from Ciga, Pec municipality, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise to my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But just looking at line 14, the witness -- the witness's answer is: "At that time what people were saying in Glodjane was that this was a training ground." Could Mr. Dutertre simply clarify which people were saying that to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I had time to ask questions, I could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask something about the shooting, the noise that you -- that was heard from Glodjane. Did you hear it personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally heard this. This started before April. Maybe even very early in 1998. And this sort of thing can be heard on a daily basis from then on. Up until that time, it had been only a sporadic occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You already answered my next two questions about the beginning of the shooting and how often they could be heard. Now, coming to the question suggested by the Defence, which I had planned anyway. How did you know there was a training ground or a training camp in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman from Irzniq, Miodrag Otovic, and Slobodan Prascevic, for as long as he was the commander, he had already left for Prascevici earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's notes: Could both the witness's microphones please be switched on. We can barely hear him. And for the interpreters, please, could the second microphone be switched on as well. We can't hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please come and sit a bit closer to the microphone because the interpreters have some difficulties in hearing you. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the answer you provided to my last question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this also from Slobodan Prascevic, from Miodrag Otovic, and Drasko Vukicevic, who was then the commander of the police station at Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When did they give you this information?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was then. Drasko Vukicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer, which trailed off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drasko, Drasko Vukicevic, he was the commander at the time back in April of 1998, the commander of the Irzniq police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And is that when he gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People used to say the same thing earlier on, but this was the first time they said it officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "people"? You say people used to say the same thing earlier on, but which people?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People around the village, neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: From which village?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratishe, Dasinovac, Ljumbarda, the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give us specific names of people saying those things?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, Ljubica Stojanovic from Dubrava, she was the first to find out about the training ground. Dubrava and Glodjane are two neighbouring villages; they're adjacent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, all the others, Goja Stijovic; that is, Konstantin Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did Konstantin Stijovic live?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljumbarda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let's move to something else. Yesterday, at the end of the afternoon, you mentioned the names of all the people who had left the area. You mentioned two women, Darinka and Vukosava. What's the surname of these women?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention them as leaving. They stayed and were later killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That was a slip of the tongue on my part. I mentioned people who stayed, indeed. Darinka and Vukosava, what was the surname of these two women?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are sisters. Vukosava was never married; Darinka was. Their last name was Vujosevic, Darinka and Vukosava. However, Darinka's married name was Kovac. Her husband's last name was Kovac, so her name was Darinka Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you know them personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In which village did they live?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ratis. This is the border between Kodralija and Ratishe, but they were on the border belonging to Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What do you known about what happened to them? And if you know anything, who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man named Muhamet from Kodralije told me. I don't know his last name. He worked for the electricity company in Decane. He bought some land in Kodralije close to them. It was in late July that they set fire to their crops and killed them. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is that something he observed himself? Was he there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so. I didn't ask him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When did you have this conversation with him, and where?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him at Decane. It was late September but I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'd like to move back to the 21st of April, 1998 in Donji Ratis. Who else was there in your house? Which other family members?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister Nada, her son Ivan, my daughter Novak, myself, and our father and mother. On that day, Milos Radunovic arrived along with his wife Milica and Slobo Radosevic. They all came to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where Milos Radunovic, Slobo Radosevic, and Milica came from?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three of them are from Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How far is Dasinovac from Gornji Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're neighbouring villages. They have a common border. The distance may be about 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: While you were at home on the 21st of April in Gornji Ratis, what did Milos Radunovic and Slobo Radosevic tell you about the situation in their own village, in the village of Dasinovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said it wasn't safe in Dasinovac but they had not harmed anyone, and there was, as a consequence, no reason for them to leave their houses because there was nothing for them to fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did they tell you about the other Serbs living in Dasinovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos specifically told me that he had been to see Milojka Markovic who also lived in Dasinovac with her two sons and her two neighbours, Zeljko and Veljko Dasic. They, too, had said the same thing, that they wouldn't leave unless they were forced to leave or were driven out by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You were there while this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at home at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When did you see Slobo Radosevic and Milos Radunovic for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same day, the 21st. It was a Tuesday. The 21st of April, 1998, that's when I last saw them, same as my parents. And Milica, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And on the 21st, after this conversation took place, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this conversation on the 21st, I picked up my sister and her son Ivan and I left for Decane. That's where they lived. I took them there and I myself travelled on to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What time was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in the afternoon, possibly 3.00 or 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And when you left your home, the persons you mention, apart from the ones who left with you, were still in your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent that night in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And the next day, which is probably the 22nd of April, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met a friend of mine and we went to Pec, from Djakovica to Pec. He was a Catholic. And I met my brother Novak, my older brother who had stayed behind, at our house on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what was the name of that friend you were with?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left with him for Pec to take a motor vehicle there on business. Duna Laka, that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you met your brother, as you said. What did your brother say to you, then? It was April the 22nd, 1998. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime around mid-day but I can't remember specifically. I asked him about the situation, what the situation was like, what people were doing over there, how our parents were doing, and he said he had left early that morning, at 6.00. Since he had to go to work, he took the bus from Pec to Decani. It was all right by the time he left home and everything was normal back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you clarify one thing. He said he left Gornji Ratis. On what day and at what time exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. He left the next day, the 22nd of April, 1998. At 6.00 a.m. he left and went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So when he left, your parents were still at home, were they? And he himself, when did he see your parents for the last time, and Slobodan Radunovic -- Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask Slobo Radosevic when he'd last seen them. They probably left and went to their own homes that afternoon when we left, and the parents, that morning, if they got up that morning; if not, then that same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't follow that question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You're not the only one in this room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please clarify the last question and answer so that we do understand what especially was asked and elicit such an answer that it's comprehensible to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a double question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I wanted to know when your brother Novak saw your parents for the last time, as well as Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not accustomed to American objections of compound questioning. It's not something we do in my jurisdiction. But that is a classic example of how not to ask a question, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, if you ask two questions at the same time intermingled, then there's a fair chance of confusion in getting the answer. Earlier, it was not a double question but a credible question. Now it's a double question. Could you please reduce that to a single question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When did your brother tell you he saw your parents for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother said on the 22nd of April. That's what he said when I saw him. I didn't ask him when he'd last seen them, but probably that morning. So probably it was the evening of the 21st, when he went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was it that he saw Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't spend the night in our house. They probably went home, so that should mean he saw them on the 21st of April. Probably later than I did. It was after I'd left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. So what did you do yourself on that day, the 22nd of April, 1998, after you had met your brother?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to Djakovica. I sat down with a mate of mine in a restaurant, this person named Duna Laka. We had taken the car there together, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you hear of anything else about Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic on that very day?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Some police officers came in saying that word had reached them of Slobo and Milos -- Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic having been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you have the name of these policemen?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milutin Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did they say who had arrested Milos Radunovic and Slobo Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said the Albanians had arrested them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What does that mean? How do you understand "the Albanians"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That probably means the Kosovo Liberation Army. Uniformed people who were turning up here and there and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once you had that information, how did you react for your parents? What were the moves you tried to take when you did try to take some, of course?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to go in and get them, but on my way I stopped by the police station in Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what did you do in the police station in Decani?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to ask around to see if it was safe to go there, if maybe they knew something about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what did the policemen tell you about the situation and the events then?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say it was no longer safe to go there. They said that in the village of Pozar, Kojo Stijovic had been taken; Konstantin Stijovic; Novak Stijovic, his son; Stanisa Radosevic; Milka Stijovic; and Stanislava Popovic; they had all been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What else happened to them exactly? Did the policemen tell you this?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask any further questions, but I did see all these people myself later. Konstantin Stijovic and Novak, as well as Stana Popovic, who was my next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise again, but the transcript does not here reflect the list of names that the witness gave. I don't know whether it's translation or transcription problem. But at line 21, the list of names does not properly reflect the testimony that the witness gave, and I wonder if Mr. Dutertre could ask him to give it again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you need it at this moment, then it's fine to further ask for it, Mr. Emmerson. Otherwise, of course, as soon as we find such an accent circumflex, then it's an indication that it will be reviewed later so that the exact names appear. But if you need them at this moment, then you may invite Mr. Dutertre to ask the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, since there is a break in the proceedings, I would interpose an objection on the multiple instances that have been in the record thus far of multiple hearsay as well as speculation with an understanding of what the Chamber's ruling has been before. But in the testimony that has occurred thus far, there have been both multiple -- instances of multiple hearsay, as well as speculative testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if Mr. Dutertre puts a question to the witness, he doesn't know whether the answer will be speculative or not. But at least, Mr. Dutertre, where you earlier said, "if I would have time to ask in more detail," you certainly are aware that if the Chamber doesn't receive more detail about hearsay, that of course this will -- this may well have consequences when evaluating the evidence. So, therefore -- and also, if you think that the witness could give us more than just speculation, then of course if you consider the information the witness provides to the Chamber of relevance and of importance to your case, then better try to find out what is speculation and what is knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am trying to hear from our witness where the information is coming from. Thank you for reminding me of this. I do share the Defence's concern that we need to have the exact names when the police mentioned that something had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And I would like our witness to repeat the names of those people; that is to say, those people who, as reported by the police, had been victims to that event.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Konstantin Stijovic, his son Novak Stijovic, Stanisa Radosevic, his daughter-in-law --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please say slowly the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters have some difficulties in hearing the names. If you are mentioning any names, would you please do it slowly so that they can follow you. Please proceed. So you mentioned -- we have now on the record, Konstantin Stijovic, his son Novak Stijovic, Stanisa Radosevic, and then his daughter-in-law by the name of ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Daughter-in-law Milka Stijovic and Stanislava Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of those people directly, yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Kojo Stijovic, his son Novak Stijovic, and Stanislava Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did Novak Stijovic tell you exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that they had been detained in the village of Pozar. They had been waiting for them there, and then they took them to Glodjane where they beat him and Stanisa Radosevic, and that they asked them to bring weapons. They left Kojo Stijovic and the others there while they went to bring weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he say who mistreated them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreters: Beat them.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask them. Kojo only told me that Mr. Haradinaj, Ramush's father, saved him and I knew this man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry, but it does seem as though Mr. Dutertre and the witness are at cross-purposes. The question at line 7 was not Did Novak Stijovic tell you? The answer between lines 8 and lines 12 are about the account given by Novak Stijovic, and the answer -- the question at line 13 is about Novak Stijovic, and the answer at line 15 is about his father Kojo Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. Line 7, question what Novak Stijovic told the witness. He then -- then the witness tells what he was told by Novak Stijovic, at least that's what I understand. Yes, that needs clarification, because the next question was -- Mr. Dutertre, was a follow-up on the first question where you invited him to -- you invited the witness to tell us what Novak Stijovic told him, and then in this follow-up question where you clearly seek an answer to what Novak Stijovic told the witness about who mistreated, then in the answer the witness switches to another source. So that should be clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, my question was to hear from you if -- whether Novak Stijovic has said who had beaten them up?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only said that they had been taken to Glodjane. He didn't mention any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. On April the 23rd, 1998, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met a neighbour of mine on that day who lived in Decani. His name was Mehmet Goga. He had a piece of land near our house, or actually he bought the land from a man called Perovic. I asked him to go to my parents' house to check up on them and to see how they were fairing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you said he had bought land close to your place, was that in Gornji Ratis or in some other place?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That land belonged to Donji Ratis. Actually, it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It belonged to Gornji Ratis. It is a piece of land between Gornji Ratis and Donji Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you met him on the 23rd and you asked him to go and visit your parents. Did he do so?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did so. I saw him three or four days later and I asked him if he had seen my parents. He said that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you met him again three or four days later, but where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, who is Tafilj Kuci?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tafilj Kuci was our neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One of your neighbours in Gornji Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Gornji Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him ever since the day he was born. He was younger than me, so I knew him since childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you meet him in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We met in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was attending post-secondary school there and I asked him to go to the house and to see what's happening with my parents. I find a car for him. It wasn't our car. I didn't want our car to be seen and recognised in the village. I borrowed a car from an Albanian friend of mine, gave him the car, and told him to go to Ratis and to check up on my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he saw and what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed to meet some four or five hours later in Decani. He told me that he was unable to go to Ratis, that he was immediately stopped in Prilep, then in Prekoluka, it's a village between Prilep and Rznic, that he had been stopped by the armed members of the KLA and that they wanted to take him to Glodjane. He told me not to go there at all because it was dangerous, and after that he came back. He hardly managed to go back. They were reluctant to release him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What day was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it was probably two or three days later, that is to say, 23rd or the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he give you other details as to what he saw when he was arrested in Prilep and then in Prekoluka?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he saw many armed men and trenches and sandbags, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where exactly? Where did he see the trenches and sandbags?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prilep and Prekoluka. There were more of them in Prekoluka, so he was unable to proceed beyond that point and he had to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did he know that the people who had arrested him were from the UCK?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. And they wanted to put a uniform on him, too. They wanted to take him to Glodjane, to give him weapons, and to keep him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he give you a description of these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And then what did you do next? What did you do to know what had happened to your parents?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I met Mehmet Goga from Decani and I sent him to Ratis. He saw my parents. They were in the house but they were unable to leave the house. Their movements were restricted. They were under guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just a clarification. The first person you sent was Tafilj Kuci and then Mehmet Goga and not the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So I come back, because we've just mentioned Mehmet Goga. Did he tell you why your parents had restricted movements?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they had been guarded by armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he give you a more detailed description of these people, of these men?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I didn't ask him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And then what did you do next to have information about your parents?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A neighbour of ours was living in Djakovica. Her name was Faza Haradinaj. Actually, her son was living in Djakovica and she was visiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So she was from Gornji Ratis, was she?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did you tell her? What did you ask her?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I went to see her son and I wanted to ask her daughter to go down there because she was younger. Her name was Fana. However, she was afraid to go and she said she didn't dare go there. Then her mother volunteered to go down there to the village, to Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What day was that, if you remember, of course, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was after Mehmet Goga. 21st. I would say 25th or 26th. I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. Can you tell us why Fana Haradinaj was afraid of going to Gornji Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she was afraid that she would come to some harm probably by the armed KLA gangs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So her mother, Faza Haradinaj, suggested she would go to Gornji Ratis herself. What did she then tell you about this visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She went with her grandson, who was seven or eight years old. However, she was unable to see my parents. She only saw armed men all over the place, and that was in the area between Prilep and Ratis. I asked her to bring at least my mother, but she said she wasn't able to bring my mother even from Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Faza Haradinaj, together with her grandson, how did they travel there? They walked there? They went by car? How did they get there?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took them to Prilep from Djakovica, and from then on they walked. She also wanted to visit her son's grave and at the same time to visit my parents. And we agreed to meet again some five or six hours later, because that was approximately the time for her -- that she needed to go to the village and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Why did you stop the car in Prilep and not further away?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had gone further, I wouldn't be alive today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, could I ask one clarifying question. You told us, Witness, that you sent both Mr. Kuci and Mr. Goga to see how your parents were. Why did you send them instead of going there yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had gone there myself, I would probably end up like my parents did. And in addition to that, I was told by the police in Pozar that there were roadblocks everywhere and that people had been taken to Glodjane, so I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do you think that Mr. Kuci and Mr. Goga did not have a similar risk, or did you think that they were at a similar risk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not in the same danger as I would be because Serbs were in great danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you suggested that they would not take your car but another car. What made your car more vulnerable than the other car? I mean, why was the risk greater if using your car than the other car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because everybody would recognise our car belonging to a Serb, and they acted differently if a car was owned by an Albanian. So in order for this person to not expose him to any greater risk, we decided to -- not to give him our car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I then well understand that there was less risk for non-Serbs to go there, and there was less risk for a car that could be identified as non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Those were exactly the questions I was going to put to wind up this part of the examination, why asking Albanian people to go and visit his parents and not go himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Going back to Faza Haradinaj, did she describe to you who were those soldiers that she had seen when she walked towards Gornji Ratis from Prilep?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't describe them. She just said that they were in uniforms. I didn't ask her to do that. I didn't think it was necessary because I never realised what was about to happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. Then, in September, what did you hear about your parents; that is, in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1998, I think it was early September, we heard that a mass grave was discovered at the end of the Radonjic canal. That's a border between Ratis and Glodjane, and this is where the canal ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And in that time did you meet someone called Saban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in Dasinovac, at his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That was in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in September, but I cannot remember the exact date. I think it was the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saban told me specifically about my parents, that they had been in their house for about 10 or 15 days. He -- our neighbour, Sulj Kuci, could have taken them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Ten to 15 days after what?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had been there. Some 10 or 15 days after the 21st of April is the period that they spent in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What else did he say about them?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also told me that Mika was living with them, that she came to her cousin. They were family friends of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please pronounce Albanian/Serbian names slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, whenever you mention a name, do it slowly because the interpreters could not follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So when you referred to Mika, who are you referring to exactly? Can you give us the family name?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her real name was Milica Radunovic. We called her Mika.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This is Milos Radunovic's wife, then?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And then after that what did Saban Sadikaj tell you about your parents and about Mika Radunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything else about my parents. He only said about his son Xhevat Sadikaj and Rustem Sadrijaj, I think their surname was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did he say about his son Xhevat?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Xhevat, Djevdet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My apologies. Djevdet Sadikaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So what did he say did Djevdet Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that some sort of a meeting had been held in their house which was by the roadside. Djevdet and all those other people who were at the meeting, Rustem and such like, they were the people who caught Milos Radunovic as he was on his way to see Slobo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What house are you referring to when you said there was this meeting in a house? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saban Sadikaj's house, or rather his son Djevdet's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You also mentioned someone else who was there. Can you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rustem "Kamisi" Sadrijaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So he said those people had seen Milos Radunovic when they went to see Radosevic. Is that something they thought themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the question doesn't make sense, at least not as translated, and it's not clear at all whether or not Saban Sadikaj was reporting things he has seen and heard or been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do have a problem with the translation here. I first said that Saban Sadikaj had said to our witness here attending that some people had caught Milos, who was going to Slobodan Radosevic, and what I asked was if this was Saban Sadikaj had seen himself. That was badly translated, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has become rather complicated. Try to put as simple as possible the question you had in mind to this witness so that he feels directly addressed by you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So has Saban Sadikaj seen that Milos Radunovic was caught when he was going to Slobodan Radosevic by those people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me at the time that he had seen it and that he had told them to leave the man alone. They had been neighbours for a hundred years. And they went after him, too. They started yelling at him and chasing him back all the way to his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What was the date for that event, according to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened right after the 21st. He didn't give me the exact date, but it was right after. The 23rd or 24th, three or four days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, who is Arifaj Madjun?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arifaj Madjun was another one of our neighbours from Gornji Ratis. He was living on the border with Rznici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Have you met him in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him about my parents. He told me they hadn't been able to save them, nor the village. He said they had been taken to Glodjane. A man named Bajram Ademi from Gornji Ratis tried to save them. His father's name was Imer but he proved unable to do that either. Milica Radunovic, too, was taken away with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he tell you who these men were, these men who took away your parents and Milica Radunovic to Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said they were armed and uniformed and he didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: He witnessed this event himself?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a river there called Ratiska and then there's a bridge there. That's where he claims this happened. That's where he saw them being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else about them?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing else. I never asked any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I don't know how much time you think you'd still need, but also in the last portion of the evidence, if you would approach the matter systematically, then we get better information. If you say, He said -- if the witness says, He said they've been taken to Glodjane, a man named so and so tried to save them, it's totally unclear where this man was when they were arrested, where -- how this man tried to save him. I take it, but that's not asked either, that this has an ethnic background so that, of course, we could guess on who is of what ethnicity. And then he said they were armed and uniformed, but we do not know where he saw them. Were they always in the same hands? It's not a precise -- and you're not insisting in your questioning on getting a precise story. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, you're supposed to finish by 4.00 and we'll then have a break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll be finished by then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, moving back to this eye-witness, where was he specifically when he saw those uniformed men taking away your parents as well as Milica Radunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was heading down the Ratis-Rznic road, near the river at the bridge. That's where he claims he saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he give you a description of the uniforms these men were wearing when they took away your parents and Milica Radunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked, nor did he tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he tell you the ethnicity of these men?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked about their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You spoke about somebody who tried to save your parents. Did Arifaj Madjun say he was present at the time, and could you give us more details about what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me he had been present and that Bajram Ademi, son of Imer, tried to save him but they tried to kill him, too. And he was in no position to save them, nor was anyone else from the village for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did that take place? Where did he try to save them?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taking them to Glodjane. It was along the Ratis-Glodjane road, near the Ratiska river. That's where they met.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Bajram Imer had taken what steps, exactly? What did he try to do with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told them not to touch them. Those were elderly people who had not harmed people and he told them to simply release them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And at the river, how did Arifaj Madjun know they had been taken towards Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know that? That's what he told me. Was it true or not is not something that I can judge. However, when we met he said, We weren't able to save them; they were taken to Glodjane. I know no more. I didn't ask and he didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have displayed on the screen exhibit number -- 65 ter 710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that got a number already, Mr. Dutertre, or does it need one? Has it been numbered?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number P28, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, could you tell us who the person on this photograph is?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my father, Milovan Vlahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to have displayed 65 ter number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number as well, Mr. ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P29, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, could you tell us who is depicted on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother, Milka Vlahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vlahovic, did you at some stage give a blood sample for DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice. For my father and for my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you learn whether your mother had been identified through DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They identified her in that way, and they sent the remains to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have displayed on our screens 65 ter document number 901, page 2. It will also need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P30, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish this exhibit to be broadcast outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, can you see your name among the various people reported to have given a blood sample for analysis?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no dispute about this evidence. As Mr. Dutertre knows, the DNA evidence is the subject of agreement in respect to this set of remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no dispute, Mr. Dutertre, that this -- I take it that then signatures, whatever we find on that document, is accepted as in conformity with reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not simply the document. The correctness of the DNA identification is the subject of an agreed fact. The evidence that's being elicited at the moment as far as, with the greatest respect, I can see is simply a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, there seems to be no dispute about this. Although we have not received a final confirmation of this to be an agreed fact, we have been now --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a few questions were asked during a previous testimony on the identification process, and given those questions, I thought that there may have been some concerns from the Defence. But I'm glad to hear today that there is no argument, and that we can actually finalise the agreed facts on these issues as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there's no dispute, I will now conclude this line of questioning on that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, there may have been problems with the usual, I would say, the traditional, identification and also perhaps through mixing up remains, but I do understand that here there's no dispute about this DNA identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarification, I didn't ask any questions of any witness about DNA identification. The questions, as Your Honour knows, that I've been asking are directed to the integrity of the Serbian recovery and forensic operation, rather than to any question of subsequent DNA analysis by international organisations, which we've indicated would be agreed now for very many months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do we also understand that there's no issue in relation to this identification as to mixing up remains or not? Okay. Not correctly identifying from whom the samples were taken and who exactly was identified. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the record is clear, we are of the same mind with regard to this set of remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey, I hardly can see you, but if you're silent, I take it that you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Silence indicates content and consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Dutertre, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm happy to see that everything's clear, but I didn't think it was that clear when Mr. Radosevic was questioned, although there had been an agreement on the DNA identification of the father of that witness. But I am glad to hear that, in fact, there's no dispute and we'll finalise everything as quickly as possible. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one relatively simple question, Mr. Vlahovic. You told us that the source of your knowledge was at the bridge over the Ratiska river. Was that where your parents were arrested or taken, or was it at any other place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My parents were arrested in their home because they had remained there. This was only the road to Glodjane. He probably just happened to be there when they were being taken away. I didn't ask him how he got to be there, but he was the one who shared this story with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What actually happened is that they saw your parents after, as you understood, they had been arrested at home, been taken in a certain direction, and at that point in the road they intervened, or at least your source of knowledge, the one who told you that someone else at that point intervened and asked to have them released. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He and Bajram Imer or Bajram Ademi. Bajram was fiercely in favour of them being released, but those other men tried to kill him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this answer. We'll have a break until 4.25. After the break, you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber was informed that you would like to address us. Could it be done in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Emmerson, may I take it that you keep a close eye on when to go into private session for the reasons you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave that entirely to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I can indicate now, that given the slippage that there's been, that I'm going to be saying to Your Honours at an appropriate moment when we break, that the sensible course would be to keep these witnesses separate overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What sort of time would Your Honours imagine the next break ought to take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next break, I would say, approximately a quarter to 6.00, and then we would have a break until -- no, perhaps a little bit later, ten minutes to 6.00, and then we'll split it in even parts. We're just trying to fully understand your last observation, Mr. Emmerson. You said, "I think I can indicate right now" -- yes, that you'll give us the indication at the next break, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I think I know what the indication is going to be already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That it would be preferable to pursue the course that Your Honours suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I don't think that there was any principal objection to that. MR. DI FAZIO: I've put everything I want to put to you about that clearly this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: The only other matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at this moment in open session and the witness is present. I don't know whether what you'd like to say is appropriately said under those circumstances. MR. DI FAZIO: I think it can be. I think it's just the comfort of the -- the comfort of the next -- is there any real possibility of dealing with any other person than this gentleman today? Because if there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand your question is when we expect to -- MR. DI FAZIO: Move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to conclude with this witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, would that be today or would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because I think it's unlikely that we will conclude before the end of the afternoon, but obviously I'm going to try to cross-examine as briefly as I can, so it's a possibility we could finish before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's a possibility, but it's not very likely. I'm sorry not to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but then I'd rather ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you will finish before 7.00, Mr. Emmerson, we will then adjourn for the day. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Well, then, I take it that the usual arrangements for the comfort of any other people can be made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, I apologise for calling you in and not paying proper attention to your presence. You'll now be cross-examined. Mr. Emmerson, I take it that you'll be the first one to start to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson is counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, can I start, please, by clarifying with you some family relationships. In 1998, you had three brothers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were their names Rade, Novak, and Goran?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you also had two sisters, one called Nadia and one called Natalia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Nadia, Nada. And Natalia is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told us that at the time you've described in the run-up to the 21st/22nd of April of 1998, that you had a home and a restaurant in Gjakova; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a flat and a restaurant in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And am I right in thinking that by the time you last saw your parents by the date on which you last saw your parents, you and all of your siblings were working either in Decane or in Gjakova?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did each of you have somewhere to live near to your place of work?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a flat and a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not simply asking about you, Mr. Vlahovic. All of your brothers and sisters were spending some of their nights sleeping near to the place of their work in either Decane or Gjakova, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nada used to live in Pec as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The thrust of my question is simply this: None of you were living all the time at your parents' home at this point, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time Novak was living there mostly, and I also spent more time at my parents' home than I did in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. No one had ever told you or your brothers and sisters that you had to leave Ratishe, had they?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one had told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned during your evidence this afternoon that from the beginning of the year, you had heard from time to time - and I think you said daily - the sound of gun-fire coming from the direction of Gllogjan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After New Year, I said intermittently, but then at the beginning of April these gun-shots from automatic weapons were heard on a daily basis coming from the direction of Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you say the beginning of April, you know that there was an incident that happened in Gllogjan on the 24th of March, don't you? Was it after that that you started to hear more frequent gun-fire coming from the training ground, as you thought it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention whether it became more frequent. What we did were -- what we did hear were gun-shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us that there came a day when your father saw men near to the house firing guns into the air. You remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I just want to be absolutely clear that we can work out the dates. I think you told us that your father told you about this incident on the Monday and that it had happened the day before, on the Sunday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that he didn't give you a description of these men; is that right, also?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you that they were on a tractor?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were on a tractor, and there was a trailer attached to the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you tell us that he said some of them were your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he give you a description of what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they were firing from automatic rifles, bursts of fire and single shots as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he give you a description of what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, and I didn't ask him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, just to be absolutely certain on dates, you're clear that your father told you this on the Monday because you'd spent the weekend away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, if I tell you that the 20th of April was a Monday, that would mean that your father had seen these men firing guns into the air on Sunday, the 19th. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, up until that time, you yourself had never been stopped by armed Albanians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And neither had any of your siblings?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: By this time, Monday, the 20th, had you ever seen groups of armed Albanians gathered on the roads in the villages around where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: By this date, had you ever seen any Albanians in uniform in the areas around your home?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the only sign of any sort of activity of this kind is the sound of gun-fire that you had heard, you say, on a daily basis from the beginning of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's not what I am saying; that is how it exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to return to your family relations for a moment. Can I ask you about the Markovic family. And I think you know, don't you, that the Markovic family were after this time, after the 20th, they were escorted out of the area by Djevdet Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but he didn't dare to escort them to Decani. He had to take another route via Bistrica, Berane and then Lausic, which means that something was happening at the time since he was afraid to take them via direct route so he had to take a bypass route.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more questions about that in a little while, but just for the time being, can we be clear, that incident with the Markovics being escorted from their home, that is something which took place after you last saw your parents, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was, I think, two days later. It may have been the Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll come to -- sorry. We will come to that incident in a little while. But I just want to ask you about the Markovic family. They lived in Dashinoc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the parents were called Dragomir and Milojka Markovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they had two sons called Branislav and Slavisa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did they have any other children?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a daughter, but she was married in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were those people that you've described, Dragomir, Milojka, Branislav, Slavisa Markovic and the daughter, were they related to your family or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Dragomir was a cousin of my mother, but she died in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Who died in 1968?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 1968, 1988. And I'm talking about Dragomir Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So Dragomir Markovic was dead in 1988?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the family that were --

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. Not in 1988, in 1998 or perhaps 1997. I think he was late in 1997, after all. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he alive or not at the time that you're telling us about when Djevdet Sadikaj escorted the family away from their home in Dashinoc two days after you last saw your parents alive? Was Dragomir still alive then or not, or had he already died?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had died already.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that the family that was escorted out consisted of his wife, Milojka; is that right? And Branislav and Slavisa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear about the relationship, Dragomir was your mother's cousin?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a distant cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. "Cousin" is a word that's caused us some difficulties in this case. To us "cousin" means the daughter or son of your uncle or aunt; in other words, that your parent is the sister or brother of their parent. Is that what you understand by the word "cousin"?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We say "uncle" or "cousin" when they're direct relatives, the brother's children or the sister's children, and we use "cousin" too to cover this when they are three or four times' removed. They're relatives, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. So Dragomir at least was a relative but not an immediate relative of your mother; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about two men called Rade Markovic and Zvonko Markovic. These two men have made statements to the Prosecution in which they refer to your parents as their uncle and their aunt. Were they your cousins in the strict sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were close relatives. My mother and their father are a brother and sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that is what we understand by "cousins," clearly. Your parents and their parents were brother and sister, your parent and their parent were brother and sister?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you see them a lot at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as a teacher from the area, you presumably knew quite a lot of the Serb families in that area quite well, did you not? You'd seen their children grow up, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew all of them in Decani municipality, although there were not many to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, that's very helpful because I want to ask you about some of the other Serb families in the area and how they are related to one another? First of all, the Stijovic family. You knew Konstantin Stijovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what was Konstantin Stijovic's wife's name?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rosa, Rosa Stijovic. But she's dead as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very roughly, how old was Konstantin Stijovic in April 1998? I don't need an exact year but just an approximate age?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 70, 68, perhaps 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Momo Stijovic was one of his sons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you've told us today that Momo Stijovic was injured during an incident in Gllogjan when the police officer called Otovic was killed. Is that the same Momo Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Please be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to know what is the reference of the transcript where this was said by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm plainly in the middle of cross-examining, not in a position to check the transcript, but it's there and we will check it overnight. But let me put the question a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll find it in a second and see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put the question a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You were interviewed on the 8th of March this year by videolink from Belgrade, weren't you? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we have a note of what you are recorded as having said in that interview. Yes? You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you're recorded as having said that Momo Stijovic was injured in the incident in Gllogjan on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, he was injured but that's a different Momo, not the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify with you. There are two Momo Stijovics; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Same last name, same first name, but they were just relatives, distant ones at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you know them both?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Now, another of Konstantin's sons was Novak Stijovic; is that correct?
