utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In a statement that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, page 11, line 15. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In a statement that you made to the Prosecution in this case, you referred to a woman called Milka, M-i-l-k-a, Stijovic, who you described as Konstantin's daughter-in-law. Who was she married to, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was married to Slavo Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Slobo Stijovic [sic]. Right. So can we just have it clear. How many sons did Konstantin Stijovic have? We've heard about Momo; we've heard about Novak. You're now telling us about Slobodan. Were there any others?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. Vojo [as interpreted] is not Slavo's son. You asked me who Milka was married to. To Slavo Stijovic. Slavo Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misheard you. It wasn't Slobodan, it was Slavo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's the husband of the daughter-in-law, Milka Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But since Milka is Konstantin's daughter-in-law, it must follow that Slavo is Konstantin's son; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. When we say "daughter-in-law," what we mean is the brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Let's just be clear. I'm going to ask you the questions from the top. How many sons did Konstantin Stijovic have?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Konstantin Stijovic had three sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you give us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, it wasn't three, it was four sons. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you give us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the eldest was called Dimitrije. They called him Ljako. I used to know him as Ljako. I think his real name was Dimitrije, but everybody called him Ljako. Momo was another one, Miodrag and Novak.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Milka was not married to any of those, was she?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Let me tell you one thing: Milka was the sister-in-law of his brother, the wife of his uncle. She's quite elderly. She must be 60 or 70 years old by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the wife of whose uncle?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cousin, relative. They're not even brothers, not directly. Slavo Stijovic and Milka's husband, they're cousins, distant ones. They're not quite directly related. The sister-in-law of his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid you're confusing me. I don't know if everybody else is clear. Who is Slavo Stijovic in this story? Because you've given us the names of four sons; none of them are Slavo. Who is Slavo?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the sons, and I told you it was Ljako. I think his name was Dimitrije but most people just called him Ljako. Then Momo, Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And who is Slavo, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavo is Milka's husband, the woman who was taken to Glodjane. And Slavo is a distant cousin, not his son. He was an elderly man. He even died in Kragujevac last year. He was 70 at least. So he wasn't his son, he was a distant cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's extremely helpful. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if we are talking about a distant cousin, a distant cousin of Konstantin or of whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Konstantin. Slavo is Konstantin -- a distant cousin, and Milka is his sister-in-law. That's at least what we used to call that sort of thing. I'm not sure what you do around here. "Daughter-in-law" is the husband's wife, and "sister-in-law" is the brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's very helpful by way of clarification. So the three people you told us, or three of the people you told us at one point were taken to Gllogjan were Konstantin Stijovic, Milka Stijovic, and Stana Popovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And Novak Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll come to those in a moment. But of those three names I've just given you, they were all elderly people, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name Danilo, D-a-n-i-l-o, Stijovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Danilo Stijovic? I think it was Momo's cousin, but he's from Vitesa [phoen], too, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you know him, Danilo?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps by sight but not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we move to the Radosevic family. I'm not going to go in as much detail into each of them, but can we move to the Radosevic family. The father was Slobodan and the mother was Rosa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They had one son we know about called Stanisa, who has given evidence in this court.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They have two sons: Radoje and Stanisa. Radoje being the elder and Stanisa being the younger son, plus four daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I ask you about the name Zeljko Radosevic, Z-e-l-j-k-o. Zeljko Radosevic, do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. He certainly wasn't from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the Radunovic family, briefly. The father was called Milos; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the mother was called Milka.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milica. You mean Milos's wife? Milos's mother's name was Dunja. I'm not sure which one you had in mind, his mother or his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I meant wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, when you are talking about Danilo, who was the cousin of Momo Stijovic, I was a bit confused because the witness earlier testified that there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Momo, he said Momo, or did I --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I asked him, and this is line -- page 66, line 1: "Does the name Danilo mean anything to you?" And he says: "I think it was Momo's cousin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But now we have two Momos.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to know whether he is the cousin of Momo, the son of Konstantin, or of the other Momo. That confused me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you answer the Judge's question, if you understand it? Was Danilo the cousin of the Momo who was the son of Konstantin, or was he the cousin of the Momo who was injured at Gllogjan on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He wasn't a cousin of Momo's son, but he was related to that Momo who was injured in Glodjane. This Momo was from Bites. So he was his relative and not the other man's relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And going back, then, to the Radunovic family. Milos and his wife Milica, can you tell us, please, the names of their children?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had three children: Lidija Radunovic, Mirko Radunovic, and Ljubisa Radunovic. Two sons, one daughter. Lidija Radunovic, Mirko Radunovic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Ljubisa.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Ljubisa Radunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And how old roughly was Ljubisa in April 1998, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1998, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-one, 32. I think he was born in 1965 or possibly 1966 or possibly 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now the Stojanovic family. You mentioned Dragoslav, and the brother who was with Dragoslav at the time of the incident you've told us about was called Mijat; is that correct? M-i-j-a-t?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. His nickname was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What was his nickname, Mijat's nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kika. Kika.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did they -- were there other brothers or was there just two brothers?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Five brothers. Could you give us the names of the other three, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predrag, last name Stojanovic, needless to say; Vesko --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is his name Veselin in full?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not certain myself. I think it's Vesko. I don't know. I think it's Vesko. Veselin is the Stijovic one. You probably have a different person in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll come -- we'll come to Veselin Stijovic in a minute, but isn't "Vesko" a short-form for "Veselin"?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Could be both.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So there was still one brother outstanding. You've told us about Dragoslav, Mijat, Predrag, Vesko. And the last one was called?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Vlado. And were these five boys all over 18 at the time that we're concerned with, in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about for the moment about family relationships. I now want to move on to another topic and to the evidence you gave us yesterday about the problems that you say had been experienced by Serb families in this area over decades leading up to 1998. And you told us yesterday, if I can take it shortly, that the Serb population had dwindled over the decades as a result of persistent harassment from Albanians. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fair summary. Let me tell you, back in 1971, one of my distant cousins, Milo Vlahovic and Atric Perovic had this happen to them. They set fire to their haystacks out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very happy for you to give us as much detail as you want, but could you just concentrate on answering the question? I will give you the opportunity, I assure you, to tell us all about it. But you agree with the summary that I've put to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in the witness statement that you made for the Prosecution in this case, you said that there had always been tension between Serb and Albanian families in the area; you said it had been like that "all my life." Is that a fair description of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always like that, but it didn't apply to all families. There were good families, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yeah, there were particular problems with particular Albanian families; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, again, I'm going to put to you some of the things that you said to us yesterday and I'll just get you to confirm the description you've given us, and if there's anything you want to add, please do. You told us yesterday that over the decades Albanians denied Serbs access to the public irrigation system; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, in my general area, yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that on occasions some Albanians would set Serb crops on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you've told us just a moment ago about one such incident that took place in the 1970s; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you said yesterday that in some areas, although not in Ratishe, Serb girls were being raped; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think you said at one point in an interview you gave on the videolink that Albanians would graze their animals on Serb property over the decades; is that right? Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was known to happen, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, these were the grievances that Mr. Milosevic was taking up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was or not, but I know what happened in my area and my village specifically. About the water-supply system, that was certainly true. And they really wrought a lot of havoc in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Were there disputes between particular Serb families and particular Albanian families about the ownership of land and grazing land that had gone back for generations?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You weren't aware of any land disputes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't. I didn't know about any particular dispute. I know that Serbs would sell their land and Albanians would buy the land. I'm not sure about any conveyance deeds or anything like that, how that worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not talking about conveyancing problems, Mr. Vlahovic. But, for example, arguments about whether it was okay for one family who was Albanian to graze their animals on another family's land, that type of thing which you've just told us about, those kind of arguments about property were common. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Things like that did happen, problems with cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, what you've described is, as you put it, a campaign of harassment going on for decades against the Serb population in that area. Is that what you're trying to convey to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that most Serb families that you knew in the area had hunting weapons at their homes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all, but many did; that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As far as you know, did the Serbs ever retaliate over the years?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of, or, rather, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And before 1997, were the Albanian families generally armed or not? Before 1997.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Albanians who had hunting rifles, but how should I know exactly who had a hunting rifle and who didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just asking you for an impression. You've told us that most Serb families had hunting weapons. It's not right, is it, that most Albanian families had hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were some who had hunting weapons, those who went hunting, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were there restrictions on Albanians owning weapons, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Let's ask you about something you do know about. You've told us that in 1991 Albanian families stopped sending their children to Serb-run schools; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Serb-run schools. They stopped sending their children to -- or, rather, they didn't accept the Serbian curriculum. They wanted an Albanian one and that's why they no longer sent their children to the same school that all the Serb children went to. The Decani state school, for example, there was an elementary school there, it was called Brotherhood in Crmljane, and then the Serbs moved to an elementary school in the downtown area, but the Albanians were left with that elementary school and they kept on using it. And more or less the same thing happened in other villages, for example, in Gramocelj where I worked. All of those were state-run schools, but only the Albanians attended. There were no Serbs or Roma people, students, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as part of the Serb state curriculum, you were teaching Serbian language to Albanian children, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had you ever been permitted to teach in Albanian at any time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to the Albanian children in Albanian? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's my question. You do understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I taught children Serbian. The rest of the instruction was in Albanian. They had their Albanian professors for mathematics, history, and all other subjects, so they had tuition in their mother tongue. They only had Serbian, just as we Serbs learned Albanian, and we had an Albanian teacher. I could have taught them, but why should that be the case if they had their Albanian teachers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want you to be very careful in your evidence on this, Mr. Vlahovic. Are you saying that throughout the 1990s, in the schools that you were aware of in the area around where you lived, it was open to Albanian families to have their children taught in Albanian, all the way through the 1990s in the schools you were working in?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said "English"? Yes, yes, yes. When I went to school, they also had tuition in Albanian. I started learning Albanian in my fourth grade, and the Serbian was just one of the subjects. The rest of the subjects were being taught in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when it was no longer permissible under the Serbian state curriculum for children to be taught in Albanian, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until September 1991. That is when the Albanians agreed to learn Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you answer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians ceased learning Serbian and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you the question again? Did there come a time when it was no longer permissible under the state -- Serbian state curriculum for children to be taught in Albanian; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What curriculum are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever any time, Mr. Vlahovic, when Albanian children were taught their history, their mathematics, whatever other non-linguistic courses, whether they received that exclusively in Serbian and that where they were not allowed to receive these lessons in Albanian? That's the question, I think, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, ever since I started working in the school, or since I've been going to school, the Albanian children were taught all subjects in the Albanian language except for the Serbian, which they started learning in the fourth grade, just as we did -- started learning Albanian in the fourth grade. So teachers and professors were all Albanians, except for those who taught Serbian. Those were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that continued during all of the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until 1991. Of course, they continued in the same manner; only they removed Serbian from their curriculum. They did not want to recognise the curriculum of Serbia but they continued to study in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other lessons - I'm focusing on history, mathematics, geography, whatever else - were the children allowed to have these lessons given in their own Albanian language after 1991? In your school, did those who were teaching geography, history, mathematics, were they allowed to speak Albanian to Albanian pupils?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were allowed. Nobody prevented them. Specifically in Ljumbarda, I can describe the situation. Children studied in Albanian and the teachers taught in Albanian, but at that time they refused to work according to the curriculum of Serbia, but they chose the curriculum of the state of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. And finally on this matter, I don't want to take up any more time on it, if I had walked into your school in 1997 with an Albanian child and said, Will you please teach this child in Albanian, what would the answer have been, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I knew the language. I was all right with that. But that had to be agreed with the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it wasn't permitted under the curriculum, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand you. What do you mean, "not permitted"?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on to another topic. The picture that you've given us of the conflicts that were taking place over the years before 1998, would it be fair at least to say that there were deep-seated resentments on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There might have been. But not with everyone, not with every family.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not saying with every family, but presumably the Serb families that you say were having their haystacks burned were pretty resentful about it, weren't they? Hmm? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about these families, some of them moved away to other parts, my uncle included.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to get a picture of what's going on at the point in time that we are discussing in April. Now, in a witness statement that you made in this case, you said that by the 18th of April, the Serb police had withdrawn from the police station in Irzniq to Baballoq some distance away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the date, but if you're asking me if they withdrew, yes, they did. They went to Babaloc.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for exactly the date, but you said in your statement that that is something that had already happened by the time you last saw your parents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, of course, you must have known, didn't you, about the incidents that had happened in Drenica, in Likoshan and in Prekaz in which 80 Albanians had been killed at the end of March -- I'm sorry, the end of February and the beginning of March. You knew about those incidents, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you obviously knew what happened in Gllogjan on the 24th of March, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'm looking at the clock. If you would find a suitable moment soon, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Once the police withdrew, you've told us that by this time members of the Albanian community had begun to acquire weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, although they started acquiring them even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So you had a number of Albanians with increasing numbers of weapons, you had a history of tensions between the communities, a number of individual disputes between families, the attacks on Likoshan and Prekaz, what happened in Gllogjan, and then the withdrawal of the police. That's the picture that we have up to the 20th of April, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in your view, Mr. Vlahovic, just to get the picture, did the withdrawal of the police in that situation, given what had happened in Gllogjan and Prekaz, given the presence of weapons, did that provide an opportunity for people with long-standing grievances against their neighbours, to be settling old scores?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it offered an opportunity, but as far as my parents were concerned, we never had any feud with anyone. We just lived in our house. I don't know about the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a convenient moment. May I make just one short observation? The name of Glodjane, of course, is very often mentioned. Very often it's quite clear that it should be the Glodjane near to Donji or Gornji Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that whenever reference is made or whenever one of the parties must consider that when Glodjane is mentioned either in the question or in the answer, which is the Glodjane just 2 kilometres north from Jablanica that we'll be alerted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If at any stage I ask anybody a question about the Gllogjan which is north of Jablanica, I will make that absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Then we will have a break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at 10 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, you've told us in your evidence about three incidents that happened in the area around Ratishe which caused tension to rise in the period prior to the 20th of April. You told us about the killing of the policeman Slobodan Prascevic, the attack on the Culafic home in Ratishe, and the attack on the Orthodox church in the village. And I just want to see if I can, with you, clarify the dates of these incidents. Now, you should know that there is agreement in this case that the police officer Slobodan Prascevic was shot and killed on the 2nd of March, so that would be between the time of the incident in Likoshan and the time of the incident in Prekaz; do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's most probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've also heard evidence from someone who was present at the time of that shooting of Slobodan Prascevic, that the attack on the Culafic home had occurred the day before. Does that sound right to you as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So that would put that incident around about the 1st of March. Now, we've also been told about an interview which was conducted with Nastadin and Jela Culafic by a lady from a non-governmental organisation, and the notes of that interview refer, when speaking to Jela Culafic, to a long-running property dispute about ownership of land between the Culafics and a particular Albanian. Now, you've told us you knew the Culafics personally. Were you aware of that property dispute yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then I want to move on to a number of different individuals, or groups of individuals, that you've told us about, and particularly individual Serb families and how they encountered armed Albanians on or about the 20th of April, all right? Now, you told us this afternoon that on the 22nd of April, you went to Decane Police Station to find out if it was safe to go to your parents' home, and that you were told by the police about five people who had been detained. And you gave us a list of names which we had to clarify: Konstantin Stijovic, Novak Stijovic, Stanisa Radosevic, Milka Stijovic, and Stanisa Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanislava Popovic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Stanislava Popovic. Now, you told us that a little later on, you had spoken directly to Konstantin Stijovic and you'd spoken to Novak Stijovic. Can I just ask you this: It wasn't entirely clear to me from your evidence. Was it your understanding from speaking to Konstantin and Novak Stijovic that all five of these people had been detained together or that there were two separate incidents of detention?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened on two different occasions, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you spoke to the two of them. Did they tell you that they'd been detained together or separately, Konstantin and Novak?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask them that, and they didn't tell me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. We've seen an interview with Konstantin Stijovic by the same non-governmental organisation and notes of an interview that took place in which he is recorded as saying that nobody hit him or any of the people with him, and that after being questioned they were released. Is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So he told you something different to that, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you were giving evidence about this, this afternoon, you said -- it became a little confused, but you said at one point that he was released when Hilmi Haradinaj, Ramush's father, intervened; is that right? Is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they slapped him on the face and that his Montenegrin cap fell down. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: His cap came off?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a result of the slapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you about being released by Hilmi Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, again, just so that we're clear, were you being told that Konstantin Stijovic, Milka Stijovic, and Stanislava Popovic, the three older people, were detained in one incident, and that Novak Stijovic and Stanisa Radosevic were detained in another incident? Is that what you were being told or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me that. I didn't inquire about whether that happened at the same time or not. We just didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And did Konstantin tell you that he was given a lift away from Gllogjan along with Milka Stijovic and Stanislava Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he was given a lift as far as Prilep. I think it was Prilep, the village of Prilep.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And all three of them were unhurt; we can agree on that, can we?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not those three. But let me add something. Stanislava Popovic said that she recognised Redzep, and when she asked me, Redzep, my son, is that you, that is when he released her.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So Redzep who?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Redzep Arifaj, father's name Osman.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the Markovic family for a moment. You started to tell us a little bit about that earlier on. They were escorted out of Dashinoc where they lived and given safe passage by a man called Djevdet Sadikaj. Is that what you understood?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milojka told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Milojka Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this man Djevdet Sadikaj, can you just confirm for the Tribunal, he is the son, isn't he, of Saban Sadikaj, the man that you spoke to later on in Dashinoc, in September?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The youngest son. Actually, they have another son, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it may matter a little later on. We'll come back to that. But you understood, did you, that Djevdet had gone out of his way to take them via a particular route so that they could safely leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you understand Djevdet Sadikaj to be, later on, a KLA commander in Dashinoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him personally. We were friends. He was the president in Dasinovac and he probably later became a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I just want to ask you about a third family that you mentioned briefly in your evidence. Radun Dabetic. Radun, R-a-d-u-n, Dabetic, D-a-b-e-t-i-c, his wife Lijlja, L-i-j-l-j-a, and their two children. Now, did you hear something about that family and how they left the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Stanisa Radosevic was returned from Glodjane, he was covered in blood and he wanted to fetch his hunting rifle from home. He -- they were his neighbours, they dropped by. And after he told them something, they went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well again, let me put to you something that you said in your witness statement and see if you can confirm that this is what you understood. In the witness statement you made in this case, you said that that family left Dashinoc on the 22nd of April, which would be the Wednesday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was on the 22nd. Most probably it was. Let me just give a minute to refresh my memory. Yes, it was on the 22nd, when those people were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in your statement you said, as I think you've just indicated, that on their way out, they came across a group of armed Albanians who detained them and searched them and then permitted them to go on their way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you some questions about the inquiries that you and your family made about your parents in the period between the 20th of April, when you last saw them, and the beginning of September, all right? So I'm asking you about inquiries that took place during that period. We'll come to what happened in September a little later on, all right? And I want to get the order correct because I think it got a little bit out of order when you were answering Mr. Dutertre's questions, although we went back over it again? First of all, is it right that the first person that you asked to make inquiries about your family was Tafilj Kuci? He was the first person; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, again, correct me if I've got this wrong, but was he a former student of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in your witness statement in this case, you said that you asked him to go on the 23rd of April; that was when you asked him, which would have been the Thursday of that week. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's right. Give me just a second, please. Yes, I think that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then you said he came back and said that he, in effect, had been turned away at Prekoluka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't just tell him to go back. They wanted to take him to Glodjane, give him a uniform and keep him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he returned he told me not to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, that was shorthand on my part. He got as far as Prekoluka and he told you that the men there had tried to persuade him to join the KLA and to put on a uniform and carry a gun, but he had come back, had not gone to Gllogjan to do that, and had gone no further than Prekoluka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you received no information about your parents from him?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because he told me he didn't manage to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the next person who you told us who you sent was Mehmet Goka [sic]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For the record, is his surname spelled G-o-k-a [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goga.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's Goga, thank you. And you said that he was from Decane but owned property close to your parents' home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to understand your evidence about this because you told us this afternoon that he came back and spoke to you again; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but it was two or three days later, not the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think in your statement you said that you asked him to go two or three days after the attempt by Tafilj Kuci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if it's two or three days later that I saw him. Maybe a day or two. But I hadn't seen him for two or three days after because I'd asked him to go there. It may have not been a wise thing to do but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just so that the Judges have it clear, there was an interval of deals between Tafilj Kuci going on your behalf and you asking Mehmet Goga to go; is that correct? An interval of some days between those two incidents; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days had passed before he told me that he had gone there. Not much time at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you do need -- I'm trying to be specific. There were two stages to this. There was an interval of days between Tafilj Kuci going and you asking Mehmet Goga to go, and then a further interval of days between you asking Mehmet Goga to go and him coming back and telling you what he had discovered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it didn't take that long. Altogether, a total of four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would be about what I was putting to you. Again, from your witness statement in this case, you suggested that when he came back to you to tell you what he'd seen, it was around about the 26th or 27th of April. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds likely. I'm not sure about the days, the 26th, the 27th, the dates. About five days altogether. I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those dates were dates that you gave to the Prosecution when you were interviewed about this in 2002, and that's where I've taken them from. So it was roughly -- roughly, was it about a week after you'd last seen your parents that he came back and told you what he had seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you say that -- you told us this afternoon that he said he'd seen your parents, that they were in the house, that their movements were restricted, and that they were being guarded by armed men. Is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want you to reflect on that for a moment, because -- and I'll put the passage if I need to, but in a witness statement that you made about this incident in April 2002, about this conversation, you told the Prosecution investigator that you couldn't remember whether or not he had said that the men were armed. You couldn't remember that one way or the other. Now, I'm going to give you an opportunity to reflect on the answer you've given. Did he say the men were armed or did he not, or can you not remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were armed. That's what he said. I'm certain about that. I didn't ask about the uniforms. But he did tell me about the weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We didn't get the last part of the witness's answer. We just trailed off.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why, in April 2002, you would have told the Prosecution investigator that you could not remember one way or the other whether he had said that these men were armed or not? Can you think of any reason why you would have said that to the Prosecution investigator?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason. Had they not been armed, had they not been guarded, they would have left. They would not just have stayed behind. I really can't think of a single reason. He may not have told me about the uniform. I didn't ask. He told me they were well. He told me that we shouldn't go there because they were under guard by armed men. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Did he tell you that there were armed men stationed at their home or just that there were armed men in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around their home. I didn't ask if they were inside the house, but they were guarding them. I didn't ask anything else. My impression was they were nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Nearby, this was your impression, that they were nearby. It's very important to be specific about this because you're describing a conversation based on what someone else told you they had seen. Now, "nearby" could mean a lot of different things and you've told us a moment ago it was your impression that they were nearby. Now, if this man had told you that there were armed guards standing on your parents' property, that's something you would have been clear about, isn't it? You would have remembered that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time I didn't know what would happen next. I, perhaps, could have tried harder to remember, but this is the best I can do. I am really not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's very important that you be accurate about this, Mr. Vlahovic. Did Mehmet Goga say to you in terms that there were armed men standing on your parents' property, or did he say -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to that question. The witness has already been taken to this point about three or four times. He's made it clear, he's made it clear what his recollection is, and the question about whether the men were on the property, whether they were standing there, has already been put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well -- MR. DI FAZIO: How many times more is Mr. Emmerson going to repeat this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just as far as I'll allow him to do that, and this question is allowed. So could you please answer the question, Mr. Vlahovic. Mr. Emmerson stressed very much that it's important to know exactly whether Mehmet Goga said to you about the presence of these men; that they were armed men standing on your parents' property. Did he say this or did he not say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said he had seen armed men guarding them, and they weren't allowed to leave. That's what he said. I didn't ask him where precisely these people were. In the house, around the house. He saw them. That's a fact. That means they were there. I asked no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So nearby -- when you said a moment ago, "my impression was that they were nearby," I mean "nearby" could have been, for example, at the nearest junction to their house, could it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere they could keep an eye on them. It couldn't have been too far away. They must have been very, very nearby. The next junction would have been too far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, we're now entering the realm of making inferences from what was said. Could you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The next step in the process, you've told us, was when you arranged to take Faza Haradinaj and her grandson and drop them off in Prilep while they walked to your parents' home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, again, just so we can get the dates clear, in your statement you put that incident as having happened on the 2nd or 3rd of May, so about two weeks after you last saw your parents; is that -- does that accord with your correction?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was earlier on, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, you were asked about this when you did the video-conference on the 8th of March and confirmed then that it was the 2nd or 3rd of May when you sent Faza Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain about the date, but I think it was earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been as you suggest. My impression is it was earlier on, and I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Now, Mr. Vlahovic, in the evidence that you gave this afternoon, you told us that when she came back, she said that she was unable to see your parents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. It's not that she was unable to see them. She saw them; she just couldn't take them away. She did see them there and she asked who from Decani had visited them, and they said Mehmet Goga, which means that they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For Your Honours' note, the relevant entry is today's transcript, page 28, line 10. But so that we have it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I take it that you've checked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, there's always the possibility of any error or translation. If that would be the case, I always invite the parties to try to find the proper place and have it verified in such a way that any doubt on that matter is taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The important point, in a sense, is for the witness to clarify what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So it's not right that she was unable to see your parents. She did have the opportunity to see them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did she tell you that she spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She saw them; she spoke to them. They weren't allowed to leave. They were in the house but were unable to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you asked her, is that right, to check whether Mehmet Goga had actually been there, to ask your parents whether Mehmet Goga had actually been there. Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And she told you that, having spoken to your parents, he had been there?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't tell them to ask if Mehmet Goga had been there. I asked about anyone from Decani having visited them, and she said Mehmet Goga had been to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. You asked her to ask your parents about that because you didn't really trust Mehmet Goga; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if they were still alive and well. This proved to me that she had seen them and that they were still around. I wanted to be 100 per cent certain on this. That's what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you just address your mind to the specific question I'm putting to you, Mr. Vlahovic. The reason, I'm suggesting to you, that you asked Faza Haradinaj to check your parents -- with your parents whether Mehmet Goga or someone from Decane had been to visit them was because you did not fully trust Mehmet Goga when he told you that he had visited them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the real reason. The real reason was to make sure that she had seen them, that they were still there, that they were still alive. That was the real, the principal, reason. If I hadn't trusted him, I would never have asked him to go there. I just wanted to make absolutely certain that they were still there. If she hadn't seen them, I wouldn't have know. It wasn't for Mehmet Goga or anyone else. That was my main reason. I knew she had seen them. I knew, therefore, that they were still alive. It wasn't about me trusting him specifically or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Can I just read to you a passage of the notes that were taken when you were interviewed by videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is, for Mr. Dutertre's note, page 5 of the proofing notes, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll read it slowly so it can be translated to you. "Mr. Vlahovic did not fully trust Mehmet Goga, so he had asked Faza Haradinaj to ask his parents if Mr. Goga had visited them, which they confirmed to Faza Haradinaj. This was around the 2nd or 3rd of May." Is that an accurate record of what you said in the videolink conference; that you had asked her to check in part because you thought Mehmet Goga might be lying to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Mehmet Goga offered himself, without me asking when we met. He wanted to go and check to see if they were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this: The passage I just read to you, Mr. Vlahovic, is it an accurate record of what you told the lawyers for the Prosecution in the video-conference or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying it. I may have said it, but I certainly didn't mean it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important thing for me was to make sure that they were still alive, and the only way to do that was for her to go and see if they were still around. So they were there. Had Mehmet Goga preceded her or not, that's another issue. The main thing for me, the principal thing, was to know that they were still around, and that's why I asked Faza to do what she eventually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Faza Haradinaj about this visit again or about your parents again?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the only news you ever received from Faza Haradinaj was that your parents were still alive in the house?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were unable to leave and were under guard by armed men wearing uniforms all over the place, trenches dug all over the place, that sort of thing, and along the whole road between Prilep and the village of Ratis, which is where she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So she told you there were armed men in trenches all along the roads and that your parents were, therefore, unable to get out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't tell me about getting out. She said they were being guarded in the house with armed men lining the road. And she said not to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did she say whether there were armed men on your parents' property?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She said there were armed men around the house, that's what she said, guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, it's an important question of specifics. "Around the house" could mean a lot of different things. Do you remember now, yes or no, whether she told you that there were armed men on your parents' property? If you don't remember, say so?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On their property. On their property around the house. I didn't ask specifically whether they were in the house, but she saw them. She saw my parents, she saw them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So she did tell you, did she, that there were armed men on the property, on your parents' property? Is that what she told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She said that they were being guarded by armed men, and that they were unable to leave. I didn't ask them if they were on the property. I was interested in them being able to leave, at least in getting my mother out of there, if my father was still unable to leave. Once she was back, she told me that she had not been able to even get my mother out of there because they were being guarded by armed men, so the armed men must have been right there and not around the actual property.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But in any event, from what she told you, no armed men had prevented her from going in to visit and speak to your parents, had they?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what she said, that they hadn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need another three minutes for another matter in the absence of the witness. Could you find a suitable moment within the next two minutes to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want, if I may, finally on this topic to put to you a section of a statement that was made by your brother Novak and ask you to confirm whether or not it is accurate. Your brother Novak made a statement to the Prosecution in this case in July 2004, in which he said: "Sometime in May 1998, I heard my parents had been taken away to a headquarters in Jablanica. I was told this from Dino Haradinaj, an Albanian neighbour, who asked his mother Faza Haradinaj to go to Gornji Ratis to check if my parents were okay, and she told Dino that when she got there, the village was empty. I heard from others that they were taken away. The last time I saw my parents alive was the 23rd of April 1998. I heard different stories from different people that my parents had been taken away, had been killed, were found alive, et cetera?" Now, that is what your brother Novak is recorded as having told the Prosecution. Did Faza Haradinaj ever suggest to you that your parents had been taken away to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. And did she ever say to you that the village was empty, Gornji Ratis, when she got there?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't say; I didn't ask. I asked about my parents. That was all I asked about, not about the village being empty or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Vlahovic. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, in courtroom II. Now since we have one procedural issue remaining, I'll ask Madam Usher now to escort you out of the courtroom. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio or Mr. Dutertre, I don't know who asked for it, but there was an issue - I don't know whether we can deal with it in open session - to do something about proofing notes for which you wanted to inform the Chamber. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I just wanted to inform the Chamber that written observations on proofing are being finalised by Mr. Re. Unfortunately, and we do apologise, we could not file them at 4.00 today as was planned originally; however, a written version of these notes will be disclosed this evening and tomorrow, as early as possible; those written observations will be filed with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the usual way of dealing with proofing notes. They are communicated to the Defence first and then to the Trial Chamber. It would, at least, be a deviation from practice, unless there's some --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think we may be speaking at cross-purposes. Mr. Dutertre, I think, is referring to the Prosecution's submissions on the procedure for the audio-taping of proofing sessions which are due in to the Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We are ready to file and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I misunderstood the expression, and I didn't listen to Mr. Dutertre in French, so "the written observations on proofing" which might be not unambiguous language. But that's understood. So we have some delay in the submissions in this respect. But it will soon be there. It will be filed tomorrow, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, tomorrow morning, as early as possible. And if you think it is useful, Your Honour, a written version could be sent by e-mail to all the parties and to the Chamber as well this very evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as it's there. And if you would like to send a courtesy copy, I cannot promise you that between 11.00 this evening and my first meeting tomorrow at 8.00 I'll start reading them, but we'll read them soon. And I certainly would not oppose against sending a courtesy copy by e-mail. I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd obviously be grateful for the Prosecution's submissions as early as possible. As I indicated a moment ago, we're ready to file. We propose to file immediately, or very shortly after we rise, and we'll provide a copy directly to the Chamber as soon as we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's understood. Thank you very much for your information. No further matter? Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second issue, Your Honour, if you'll allow me. The Prosecution is writing written observations as well in order to receive in advance the documents that the Defence wishes to use during the cross-examination of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, then, that that will be part of your submissions and you are seeking reciprocity in some respect. Is that what I have to understand? We'll see and read it and -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think again there may be a crossed wire here. On Monday, Your Honours will recall, we filed a document setting out a suggested procedure for the notification each Wednesday of the witnesses the Prosecution was proposing to call. It's a different process from the proofing notes. And Mr. Re indicated that he would wish to use that suggestion as an opportunity to ask Your Honours to order that the Defence should give advance notice to the Prosecution of exhibits that they might wish to cross-examine a witness on, and it will come as no surprise to Your Honour that we will have some strong submissions to make in response to that. But that is a separate exchange of pleadings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. First of all, the Chamber appreciates that we get announced if there's any delay, et cetera, et cetera. At the same time, perhaps at this time of the day, I'm not sharp enough anymore to make a distinction between all what we can expect. Perhaps the best way is, then, to leave it to us to read it first, but of course we're quite happy, if there are any delays, that notice is given to the Chamber so that the other party can respond, if necessary. These kind of delays of half a day, I would say, would not be dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I have ten seconds of Your Honours' time before you rise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply this: This cross-examination is taking longer than I had hoped. I simply want to get an indication from Your Honours in advance of how long you would feel comfortable for me to continue, because I don't want to put myself in a position where Your Honours indicate to me that I have tried your patience. And so I would expect to be able to complete within the hour tomorrow, but that is longer than I had indicated, and so I wanted to raise it with you, and if Your Honours were of the view that it should be shortened, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're able to finish within the hour tomorrow, even if it's longer than indicated, the Chamber will accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
